fasila-hope.title: “Let him plant it”: hope and action even in the darkest moments
participants: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
fasila-hope.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ illustrated the value of continuing beneficial work however hopeless circumstances seem, with a powerful example: “If the Hour is established and one of you has a sapling in his hand, then if he can plant it before the Hour is established, let him plant it” — meaning that even if the end of the world itself were imminent, planting that small palm is worth completing.
fasila-hope.historicalContext: One of the hadith urging continued good and beneficial work however hopeless or futile outside circumstances may appear.
fasila-hope.problemType: Despairing of the point of work or effort in circumstances that seem utterly hopeless
fasila-hope.responseType: An extreme image (the end of the world) to prove that beneficial work has value even in the darkest imaginable circumstances
emotionsAddressed: Despair about the point of individual effort in the face of huge problems
Feeling that small work is worthless in the face of a major crisis
principles: The value of beneficial work is not measured by a guaranteed result, but by the act itself
Even in the most hopeless scenarios, good work keeps its meaning
Despair is no reason to stop beneficial work, however distant or impossible the result seems
modernApplications: Do not let the sheer size of a problem (environmental, social, personal) stop you from doing what you can now, however small
Keep up your useful daily work even if you feel the general situation around you is getting worse
Judge your actions by “is this beneficial?”, not by “will this change everything?”
behaviorObservations: He used the most extreme possible image of hopelessness (the end of the world) to show that beneficial work goes beyond even that scenario
whatToAvoid: Turning this meaning into a justification for ill-considered work or ignoring real consequences
fasila-hope.reflection: When even the very last possible moment is still worth a beneficial act, every moment before it gains double meaning.
keywords: i feel my effort is pointless
why do anything if the result is hopeless
i despair of change

climate anxiety

rifq-adam-intiqam.title: He never struck a woman or a servant: gentleness and leaving personal revenge
participants: ‘A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), the narrator
rifq-adam-intiqam.eventDescription: ‘A'ishah described the Prophet's ﷺ character with those around him: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant, except when fighting in the path of Allah. And he never took revenge for anything done to him, unless one of Allah's sanctities was violated, in which case he took action for Allah's sake,” showing that he completely distinguished between offence directed at him personally, which he pardoned, and the violation of Allah's sanctities, for which he became angry.
rifq-adam-intiqam.historicalContext: One of the deepest testimonies to his daily character at home and in society, narrated by the person closest to him.
prophetTraits: Distinguishing personal rights from Allah's rights
rifq-adam-intiqam.problemType: Suffering a personal offence or harm and wanting revenge for your personal dignity
rifq-adam-intiqam.responseType: A clear separation between offence directed at oneself (pardoned) and violation of public rights or Allah's sanctities (cause for anger)
emotionsAddressed: The urge to take revenge for a personal offence
Confusing defending yourself with defending a principle
principles: Not taking revenge was not weakness, but a conscious distinction between two different kinds of offence
Legitimate anger is anger for Allah's sanctities and public rights, not for personal dignity
Exemplary self-control is built through daily repetition, not one moment
modernApplications: Before responding to a personal offence, ask yourself: is this defending a public right, or only my ego?
Separate your right to set boundaries with someone who offends you from emotional revenge against them
Keep your real anger for situations where values or rights worth defending are violated
notToApplyTo: This does not mean not setting boundaries with someone who repeatedly offends you; the distinction is between emotional revenge and legitimate self-protection
behaviorObservations: He never struck anyone with his hand outside of battle
He clearly separated personal offence against him (he forgave) from violation of Allah's sanctities (he was angered)
He kept this pattern his whole life, not in one exceptional moment
whatToAvoid: Confusing giving up personal revenge with giving up public rights that must be defended
rifq-adam-intiqam.reflection: When your ability to forgive becomes deeper than a moment of weakness and turns into a firm principle, the very meaning of strength changes.

rahma-atfal-aqraa.title: “What can I do if Allah has removed mercy from your heart?”: mercy to children is a sign, not a luxury
participants: ‘A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), the narrator
rahma-atfal-aqraa.eventDescription: A bedouin came to the Prophet ﷺ and said in surprise: Do you kiss your children? We do not kiss them. The Prophet ﷺ answered with strong disapproval: “What can I do for you if Allah has removed mercy from your heart?”, showing that a lack of mercy towards children is not firmness, but a deficiency deserving disapproval, not pride.
rahma-atfal-aqraa.historicalContext: This situation describes the culture of some desert people who saw showing tenderness as weakness, and the Prophet ﷺ corrected this idea directly.
rahma-atfal-aqraa.problemType: Seeing tenderness towards children as weakness or unfitting for a serious father or mother
rahma-atfal-aqraa.responseType: Explicitly rejecting the person who takes pride in lacking mercy, instead of accepting it as a valid parenting choice
emotionsAddressed: Embarrassment at showing tenderness to one's children in front of others
Believing that harshness proves serious parenting
principles: Lack of mercy towards children is a real deficiency deserving disapproval, not a neutral personality trait
Showing tenderness does not contradict any social standing or image of “seriousness”
Mercy towards children is a measure by which a person's heart is tested in general
modernApplications: Do not be shy about showing tenderness and affection to your children in front of others
Review any inherited idea linking “firm parenting” with not showing feelings
If you see someone proud of being harsh with their children, remember this is clear Prophetic disapproval, not an alternative parenting style
notToApplyTo: This does not mean no firmness in upbringing when needed; mercy here concerns showing affection, not leniency in discipline
behaviorObservations: He rebuked the bedouin with a reproachful question, not just calm advice
He linked the lack of mercy to divine removal, not to a neutral personal choice
whatToAvoid: Thinking this hadith means total leniency in raising children without limits
rahma-atfal-aqraa.reflection: When the leader rebukes someone proud of a hard heart, it becomes clear that mercy is not optional in the moral system, but one of its pillars.
keywords: is showing affection to my children weakness
my father never showed us feelings
is being strict and harsh in parenting better
how to express my love to my children
hugging my kids

jud-ramadan.title: More generous than the free-blowing wind: generosity as a way of life
participants: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them), the narrator
jud-ramadan.eventDescription: Ibn ‘Abbas described the Prophet's ﷺ constant generosity: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the most generous of people, and he was most generous in Ramadan when Jibril met him. Jibril met him every night of Ramadan to study the Quran with him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was more generous in doing good than the free-blowing wind,” describing a generosity that renews and grows in seasons of good, not limited to one occasion.
jud-ramadan.historicalContext: One of the descriptions combining constant generosity (the most generous of people) with generosity that rises in blessed times (Ramadan).
prophetTraits: Making the most of blessed seasons
jud-ramadan.problemType: Treating generosity as an occasional event instead of a constant way of life
jud-ramadan.responseType: Describing a generosity that is constant first, and then increases in blessed seasons
emotionsAddressed: Feeling that generosity is only for certain occasions
Falling short in constant giving outside religious seasons
principles: True generosity is a constant state before it is seasonal behaviour
Blessed seasons are a time to increase one's usual giving, not to start giving that did not exist
Generosity includes giving time and knowledge, not only money
modernApplications: Make generosity a small, constant daily habit, not behaviour tied to one occasion a year
Use special times or seasons in your life to increase your existing giving, not to begin giving that was not there
Widen your idea of generosity to include your time, knowledge and help, not only money
behaviorObservations: He is described as “the most generous of people” in general before Ramadan is singled out
His growing generosity is linked to meeting Jibril and studying the Quran, that is, to increased closeness to the source of good
whatToAvoid: Considering seasonal giving enough to replace a pattern of constant giving
jud-ramadan.reflection: When generosity is a permanent state that rises in blessed seasons, it is entirely different from generosity summoned only when the occasion demands.

sabr-sadma-oula.title: “Patience is at the first shock”: patience in the moment of pain, not after
participants: A woman weeping at a grave
Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
sabr-sadma-oula.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ passed by a woman weeping bitterly at a grave and said to her: “Fear Allah and be patient.” Not recognising him, she answered sharply: “Leave me alone, you have not been struck by my calamity.” When she later learned it was the Prophet ﷺ, she came to his house to apologise, and found no doorkeepers to stop her. She said: I did not recognise you. He answered without rebuke: “Patience is only at the first shock.”
sabr-sadma-oula.historicalContext: A moving situation combining the teaching of patience with a practical model of tenderness towards someone who acts sharply in intense pain.
sabr-sadma-oula.problemType: A recent loss of a loved one, and reacting sharply to someone who tries to comfort you without meaning harm
sabr-sadma-oula.responseType: Defining patience as something that begins at the first moment of shock, with complete tolerance for the sharp reaction born of pain
emotionsAddressed: Guilt over a sharp reaction you had in a moment of intense pain
Thinking patience means showing no grief at all
principles: True patience is tested at the first moment of shock, not after the feelings calm down by themselves
A sharp reaction born of real pain does not deserve blame or rebuke
True comfort includes tolerating how a person receives it in their moment of pain
modernApplications: If in a moment of intense pain you answered sharply someone who tried to comfort you, do not burden yourself with excessive guilt; it is human and understandable
If you try to comfort someone in pain and they react sharply, remember it does not deserve to be held against them
Work on patience from the first moment of shock instead of waiting until you “get used to” the loss to show patience
behaviorObservations: He did not hold the woman's sharp reply against her when she did not recognise him
He did not stop her from reaching him later
He reframed the meaning of patience in one concise, deep sentence
whatToAvoid: Thinking a sharp reaction at the first shock cancels a person's patience or deserves blame
sabr-sadma-oula.reflection: When patience is defined as an act of the first moment rather than a result of time, it becomes closer to people and less judgemental of them.

i feel guilty about how i reacted to the tragedy
how to accept the grief of someone who just lost a loved one

sidq-yahdi.title: Truthfulness leads to righteousness: when habit becomes identity
participants: ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
sidq-yahdi.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ explained that truthfulness is not an isolated virtue but a complete path that leads a person step by step towards uprightness: “Hold fast to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. A man keeps telling the truth and striving for truthfulness until he is recorded with Allah as truthful.” And he warned that lying leads by the same logic to wickedness and then the Fire.
sidq-yahdi.historicalContext: One of the concise comprehensive sayings showing the cumulative long-term effect of truthfulness and lying on a person's character.
sidq-yahdi.problemType: Taking a small lie or partial truth lightly, as not worth worrying about
sidq-yahdi.responseType: Depicting truthfulness and lying as two cumulative paths, each step leading to the next
emotionsAddressed: Justifying a small lie as not worth worrying about
Not realising the cumulative effect of small habits on identity
principles: Truthfulness and lying are not isolated acts but cumulative paths that shape a person's identity over time
Repeated truthfulness makes a “truthful one”, as repeated lying makes a “liar”; identity is the result of repetition, not one event
Truthfulness is described as “leading” — it naturally guides towards more good, not just itself
modernApplications: Do not belittle a repeated “small” lie; its effect accumulates on your character, not just on one situation
Strive for truthfulness even in small details (excuses, descriptions, promises), not only in big issues
Ask yourself regularly: are my small speech habits building me towards truthfulness, or getting me used to justifying lies?
behaviorObservations: He did not just command truthfulness, but explained its cumulative mechanism step by step
He set the path of truth against the path of lying in the same linguistic structure to highlight the parallel
whatToAvoid: Belittling a lie just because it will not be discovered, ignoring its cumulative effect on character
sidq-yahdi.reflection: The deepest thing in this hadith is that it describes not one act, but how our identity is shaped by the accumulation of our small repeated actions.
keywords: is a small lie a problem

how to become a more honest person
the effect of repeated lying on character

uhud-injury.title: “Not for you is the decision”: when the leader is physically wounded
participants: Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her)
‘Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him)
uhud-injury.eventDescription: At the Battle of Uhud the Prophet ﷺ was badly wounded: his face was cut, a tooth was broken, and blood flowed from his head. His daughter Fatimah washed the wound while ‘Ali poured water. In the moment of pain he said in amazement: “How can a people succeed who have wounded the face of their Prophet?” and was about to pray against them, when Allah's words were revealed: “Not for you is the decision at all.”
uhud-injury.historicalContext: One of the most physically painful moments in the Prophet's ﷺ life. Commentators differed on the exact cause of the verse's revelation, between this situation and a similar one in the same context.
prophetTraits: Controlling one's reaction to physical pain
uhud-injury.problemType: Suffering physical harm or grave injustice that stirs an immediate, natural desire to pray for revenge or punish the one responsible
uhud-injury.responseType: Submitting to Allah's command despite intense pain, remembering that the final judgement on people is not in the hands of the one in pain, however wronged
emotionsAddressed: The immediate urge for revenge in physical pain or severe injustice
Feeling that an emotional reaction in a moment of pain is entirely justified
principles: Intense pain may push even the most truthful person to want to pray for harm; the feeling is not blamed, but the action is restrained
The final judgement on whether people deserve punishment or guidance is not in the hands of the one who suffered, but Allah's
Submitting to the divine command in the most painful moments is one of the deepest meanings of faith
modernApplications: When you suffer deeply from an injustice, allow yourself to feel anger without letting it finally decide the other person's fate
Remember that wanting to see the one who wronged you punished is human, but carrying out that judgement is not always in your hands
Separate treating your wound and claiming your right from the final judgement on the fate of the one who hurt you
notToApplyTo: This does not mean giving up claiming your right or defending yourself; the verse concerns the final judgement on people's fate, not seeking justice
behaviorObservations: He did not hide his pain or his first desire to pray against them
He accepted the divine guidance at once and stopped the prayer for revenge
He continued his mission despite the severe wound
whatToAvoid: Thinking that feeling a desire for revenge in intense pain deserves blame in itself; blame is for actions, not feelings
uhud-injury.reflection: When a person is reminded at their most painful moment that the judgement is not theirs, submission becomes the deepest level of faith, not just swallowing anger.

al-ifk.title: The slander incident: patience under a false accusation
participants: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him)
al-ifk.eventDescription: A false rumour spread in Madinah accusing ‘A'ishah, the Prophet's ﷺ wife, of something she was innocent of, and several Muslims took part in spreading it, including Mistah ibn Uthathah, a relative of Abu Bakr whom Abu Bakr supported financially. A whole month of pain and waiting passed without the Prophet ﷺ judging emotionally, until Allah revealed ‘A'ishah's innocence in verses of Surah al-Nur. Then Abu Bakr swore he would no longer spend on Mistah after what he had done, and a verse was revealed calling him to forgive, so he immediately resumed his support.
al-ifk.historicalContext: One of the hardest personal and social crises the Prophet ﷺ went through, because it touched his home, his wife and the reputation of the whole community; Allah devoted verses of Surah al-Nur to it.
al-ifk.problemType: Facing a false accusation that touches your reputation or that of those closest to you, spreading among people with no immediate way to prove your innocence
al-ifk.responseType: Patience and not judging hastily in the most sensitive matters, waiting until the truth becomes clear
emotionsAddressed: Intense pain from a false accusation touching reputation or family
The urge for an immediate, decisive reaction before the whole truth is clear
principles: The more personally sensitive the matter, the greater — not lesser — the need to verify
Patience under a false accusation is one of the hardest trials, because it touches reputation, not just body or wealth
Forgiving someone who did grave harm (like taking part in the rumour) is possible once the truth is established, and kindness deserves to be resumed rather than cut off forever
modernApplications: If you face a rumour or false accusation, resist the urge to react immediately, and give time and the truth a chance to appear
Do not judge someone accused in a sensitive matter based on rumour alone, without verifying
If someone harmed you gravely and then their error became clear or they repented, consider whether resuming kindness with them is possible
notToApplyTo: This does not mean every accusation will necessarily be proven false; the lesson is the method of verifying and patience while waiting, not the outcome of every similar case
behaviorObservations: He did not pass a hasty judgement throughout the time of waiting for revelation
He did not handle the crisis with personal agitation, although it touched his own home
After forgiveness was revealed in the Quran, Abu Bakr immediately resumed the kindness he had cut off
whatToAvoid: Judging someone accused in a sensitive matter based only on how widely the talk has spread
al-ifk.reflection: When the most personally painful matter is the very one that calls for the most patience and verification, it becomes clear these two qualities are tested not in the easy but in the hardest.

anas-taakhkhur.title: “Unays, did you go where I told you?”: when the one serving you is late with a task
subCategories: Dealing with those under your responsibility
participants: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), then a young boy
anas-taakhkhur.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ sent Anas ibn Malik, a young boy serving him, on an errand. Anas went out intending to go, but passed some boys playing in the market and got caught up with them. The Prophet ﷺ came and found him there, and took hold of the back of his neck from behind. Anas turned and found him laughing, and he said gently: “Unays, did you go where I told you?” He answered: Yes, I am going, O Messenger of Allah.
anas-taakhkhur.historicalContext: One of Anas ibn Malik's hadith describing the Prophet's ﷺ daily treatment of him as a young boy in his service.
anas-taakhkhur.problemType: Someone under your responsibility being late with a simple task because of a passing distraction
anas-taakhkhur.responseType: A gentle surprise instead of a scolding, a smile instead of anger, with calm guidance that brings the person back to the task
emotionsAddressed: Annoyance at a small delay or shortcoming by someone under your responsibility
The urge to escalate a simple situation that does not deserve it
principles: Not every small delay or shortcoming deserves an angry reaction
Gentle playfulness can be more effective at correcting than direct rebuke
Knowing a person's nature (a young child drawn to play) is part of dealing with them well
modernApplications: If an employee or child is late with a simple task because of a passing distraction, try a gentle approach before escalating
Remember that the people you deal with are human, with natural impulses that do not always deserve anger
Use humour sometimes in correcting instead of excessive seriousness in every situation
notToApplyTo: This does not apply to repeated or serious failings that need a more serious approach
behaviorObservations: He surprised him with a gentle touch, not an angry voice
He was laughing when he faced him, not frowning
He settled for a simple question directing him to the task, without reproach
whatToAvoid: Assuming every small delay deserves the same seriousness and escalation
anas-taakhkhur.reflection: Sometimes a smile while correcting has a stronger effect than the most serious words.

sirr-anas.title: “It is a secret”: keeping secrets even within the family
participants: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)
sirr-anas.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ sent Anas ibn Malik — still young and playing with other boys — on a private errand, and Anas came home late to his mother because of it. When he returned she asked: What kept you? He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me on an errand. She asked: What was it? He answered: It is a secret. His mother said: Never tell anyone the secret of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Anas later said: By Allah, if I had told anyone, I would have told you.
sirr-anas.historicalContext: A situation simple on the surface, but revealing a double upbringing: the Prophet's ﷺ trust in confiding a secret to a young boy, and the mother who strengthened in him the value of keeping a trust, even from her.
sirr-anas.problemType: Knowing information or a secret that belongs to someone else, under social or family pressure to reveal it
sirr-anas.responseType: Complete commitment to keeping the secret even with those closest, and instilling this value through upbringing
emotionsAddressed: Pressure to reveal a secret to someone close whose request is hard to refuse
Feeling that keeping a secret from family in particular is improper
principles: Keeping a secret has no exception for close relationships like family
The Prophet ﷺ entrusting a young boy with a secret shows his confidence that trustworthiness can be taught from a young age
The commitment to keeping a secret stays firm even after many years
modernApplications: If someone entrusts you with confidential information, keep it even from those closest to you unless there is a compelling reason to disclose
Teach your children the value of keeping secrets and being trustworthy with words from a young age, through real experience, not just advice
Do not use emotional closeness as pressure to reveal a trust that should be kept
notToApplyTo: This does not include secrets whose concealment causes real harm or violates another person's rights or safety
behaviorObservations: He entrusted a young boy with a private matter without hesitation
He did not repeat the request or check on his secrecy, but trusted him
whatToAvoid: Considering a parent's request enough justification to reveal a trust that should be kept
sirr-anas.reflection: When trustworthiness is built in childhood through a real, trusted experience, it becomes part of a person's character that stays with them for decades.
